content: The evidence review combined data from multiple cohorts with varying follow-up durations after the initiation of tuberculosis (TB) treatment. The follow-up period was divided into two phases: the time from treatment initiation to completion and the time from treatment completion to the end of follow-up. For shorter treatment regimens, post-treatment follow-up was particularly critical due to the potential for higher relapse rates, which may result from incomplete eradication of Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Follow-up was limited to 24 months after treatment initiation across all cohorts. No analyses included both intervention and comparator cohorts with follow-up exceeding 24 months. Evidence from TB treatment trials indicates that most recurrences occur within 6 to 12 months after stopping treatment. Primary analyses were designed to maximize the number of participants included in both groups, particularly for shorter regimens (6–9 months), to capture relapse events. Additional sensitivity analyses were conducted to evaluate the impact of follow-up time on treatment outcomes. The evidence informing the PICO (Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcome) questions was derived from two trials: TB-PRACTECAL and ZeNix. These trials included data from 419 of 423 participants in four arms of TB-PRACTECAL and 172 of 181 participants in four arms of ZeNix. Data from relevant trial arms were used to inform conclusions and recommendations regarding the use of the BPaL (bedaquiline, pretomanid, and linezolid) and BPaLM (bedaquiline, pretomanid, linezolid, and moxifloxacin) regimens. Some participants were excluded due to unconfirmed rifampicin resistance. In the ZeNix trial, the BPaL regimen with linezolid 1200 mg daily for 9 weeks (BPaL 1200–9) was compared to the same regimen with linezolid 1200 mg daily for 26 weeks (BPaL 1200–26) in patients with multidrug-resistant or rifampicin-resistant TB (MDR/RR-TB), with or without fluoroquinolone resistance. The primary analysis was conducted at 12 months post-treatment initiation. The benefits of BPaL 1200–9 were judged to be small, while the undesirable effects were moderate compared to BPaL 1200–26. The certainty of evidence was very low, and the panel concluded that the balance of health effects likely favored BPaL 1200–26. Similarly, the ZeNix trial compared BPaL with linezolid 600 mg daily for 26 weeks (BPaL 600–26) to BPaL 1200–26. The benefits of BPaL 600–26 were considered moderate, and the undesirable effects were deemed trivial compared to BPaL 1200–26. The certainty of evidence was very low, and the panel concluded that the balance of health effects likely favored BPaL 600–26. Based on this, the use of 26 weeks of 600 mg linezolid was suggested over 26 weeks of 1200 mg linezolid as part of the BPaL regimen in adults with MDR/RR-TB or pre-extensively drug-resistant TB (pre-XDR-TB). The TB-PRACTECAL trial compared the BPaLM regimen to longer WHO-recommended regimens for MDR/RR-TB, including 9–12-month injectable-containing regimens and 18–24-month all-oral regimens. The primary analysis was conducted at 72 weeks post-treatment initiation. The benefits of BPaLM were judged to be large, and the undesirable effects were trivial compared to the longer regimens. The certainty of evidence was very low, and the panel concluded that the balance of health effects likely favored BPaLM. Additional data on the pharmacokinetics and toxicity of linezolid and pretomanid were reviewed. Linezolid toxicity, particularly at higher doses and longer durations, is well-documented, and strategies to mitigate this are being explored. New data on pretomanid's reproductive toxicity, including hormone evaluations and a paternity survey, alleviated concerns about adverse effects on male fertility observed in animal studies. An ongoing study assessing semen in men undergoing pretomanid treatment aims to address remaining concerns. Cost-effectiveness analyses indicated that BPaL and BPaLM regimens are cost-saving compared to longer regimens, primarily due to reduced time in care and fewer outpatient visits, inpatient bed-days, and laboratory tests. The panel judged that cost-effectiveness likely favors BPaL and BPaLM. The shorter duration and reduced complexity of these regimens were also considered likely to improve equity, acceptability, and feasibility, particularly in underserved settings. Stakeholders appreciated the reduced workload and financial burden on healthcare systems but emphasized the importance of addressing safety monitoring and regulatory requirements. These regimens are likely to be cost-effective, acceptable, and feasible, with potential benefits for equity and healthcare system efficiency.
